lectures.name: Introduction to MSK Anatomy
lectures.title: Introduction to MSK anatomy
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Upper motor neuron weakness = increased tone, brisk reflexes, Babinski present · lower motor neuron = normal or low tone, reduced reflexes · MSK weakness has no objective sensory loss. Weakness without pain is uncommon. Concentric shortens, eccentric lengthens, isometric doesn't move. Hilton's law: the nerve to the muscle is the nerve to the joint. Joint pain comes from the capsule, ligaments and bone, not the cartilage.

The vocabulary the rest of the musculoskeletal (MSK) block is built on. The one clinical question it sets up: when a patient says a limb is "weak", is it pain, muscle, nerve or spinal cord?
1. Weakness: pain, muscle, or nerve?

• Weakness is a very common complaint whenever there is pain
    • pain with or without weakness is common · weakness without pain is not, which narrows the differential
    • true weakness can come from anywhere between the brain and the joint
    • a sensory problem points higher up (brain, nerve) · no sensory change → more likely muscle

cols: Upper motor neuron (stroke, spinal cord injury)
rows: Acute (Achilles rupture) or chronic (rotator cuff degeneration)
Sensory loss in the same nerve's territory
Sensory loss in the matching territory
Only that muscle (others may look weak from pain)
Lost only at the ruptured tendon

blocks.html: • Degenerative vs inflammatory pattern of joint pain

rows: Pain with activity, better with rest · gradual onset · ± stiffness through the day · ± locking or instability · may be weak · swelling only secondary
Pain at rest · morning stiffness · swelling, warmth, redness · ± rash · malaise · fever, weight loss (especially infection) · acute or subacute onset

blocks.html:
• Pattern for any MSK treatment plan
    • education
    • no red flags → non-drug first: relative rest · RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) · heat, cold, ultrasound, laser · acupuncture, yoga, massage · rehabilitation · gait aids, braces (orthoses)
    • then drugs or surgery if needed: topical (lowest dose) → injected → systemic (e.g. ibuprofen)
    • plan follow-up, contributing factors, activity restrictions
  • Describe the impact at three levels: impairment (body structure or function) · activity limitation (tasks the person can't do) · participation restriction (life roles they can't fill)
2. Development: dermatomes and myotomes

• Paraxial mesoderm forms paired somites, each supplied by one spinal nerve
    • the dermomyotome splits into a dermatome (→ skin) and a myotome (→ muscle)
  • Myotome = the muscles supplied by one root · myotomes fuse, so most muscles get more than one spinal segment (e.g. diaphragm C3-C5)
  • Dermatome = the skin supplied by one root · neighbouring dermatomes overlap, so test the middle of a dermatome
  • Two separate skin maps: dermatome (one spinal nerve, e.g. C5) vs peripheral nerve territory (one named nerve, e.g. axillary nerve)
3. Somatic nervous system

• Carried by all spinal nerves and some cranial nerves
    • general sensory fibres: pain, proprioception, temperature, pressure, touch from skin, muscle and joints
    • general motor fibres: to skeletal muscle
  • Who supplies what
    • dorsal rami → deep back muscles + skin of the back
    • ventral rami → everything else: back of the head, neck, upper limb, trunk wall, perineum, lower limb
    • cranial nerves → skin and muscles of the face
  • Reflex arc: sensory neuron into the dorsal horn → motor neuron out to the muscle (review 04 - Introduction to the Nervous System)

blocks.cap: Reflex arc: the sensory neuron enters through the dorsal root ganglion, the motor neuron leaves through the ventral root to the muscle

blocks.html: 4. Muscle contractions and the kinetic chain

rows: Lifting a dumbbell in a curl

blocks.html:
• Open kinetic chain: the limb is free (biceps curl, bench press)
  • Closed kinetic chain: the limb is fixed (push-up, walking, squatting) · more common in daily life · rotation at one joint forces the others to rotate, so biomechanics matter

blocks.cap: Isometric (no length change) vs isotonic concentric (shortening) and eccentric (lengthening)

blocks.html: 5. Joints

• Laws of joints
    • any muscle that crosses a joint acts on that joint
    • Hilton's law: the nerves supplying the muscles that move a joint also supply its sensation
  • Stability comes from 3 things: shape of the surfaces · ligaments · muscles
  • Synovial joints are the most common and are freely movable
    • hyaline cartilage and synovium are poorly innervated · joint pain comes from the capsule, ligaments and bone
    • ligaments = thickenings of the fibrous capsule where it needs reinforcing

rows: Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction (more range than condyloid)
Knee (medwiki) · knuckle (metacarpophalangeal) (sources differ - check the slides)

blocks.cap: The six synovial joint types: plane, pivot, hinge, saddle, condyloid, ball-and-socket

blocks.html: 6. The skeleton and bony terms

• Anatomical position: standing upright, face, palms and toes forward
  • Axial skeleton: skull (only freely movable joint = temporomandibular) · vertebral column (bigger lower down; coccyx not weight-bearing) · sternum · 12 pairs of ribs (lowest 2 floating)
  • Appendicular skeleton: pectoral girdle (clavicle, scapula) → humerus → radius, ulna → carpals → metacarpals → phalanges (thumb 2, other digits 3) · pelvic girdle → femur → patella (a sesamoid bone in a tendon) → tibia (weight-bearing), fibula → tarsals → metatarsals → phalanges
    • the sacroiliac joint barely moves · it hurts when it does (e.g. pregnancy)

rows: head (rounded end on a neck) · condyle (rounded distal end) · facet (small flat surface)
trochanter (femur only) > tuberosity > tubercle · process · protuberance · epicondyle (beside a condyle) · crest > line · spine
groove · notch (edge) · fossa (shallow basin) · sulcus (narrow crevice)
ramus (flat branch at an angle) · neck · sinus (air-filled cavity)

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Back & Neck
lectures.title: Anatomy of the back and neck
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperextension; the narrow posterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperflexion (which is why discs bulge out beside it). Cervical = transverse foramina + bifid spines · thoracic = costal facets + long downward spines · lumbar = big bodies. C1 nods "yes", C2 turns "no"; no disc between them. Trapezius = cranial nerve XI · deep back muscles = dorsal rami. Erector spinae → lifting strains · transversospinalis → rotation strains.

Every structure here is a possible pain generator in the next lecture. Learn what makes each region's vertebrae different, which ligament stops which movement, and which back muscles a strain hits.
1. The vertebral column

• Jobs: protect the spinal cord · carry body weight · posture and movement (flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation)
  • 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 sacral (fused into the sacrum) · 4 coccygeal (fused into the coccyx)
  • Curves absorb stress and protect the back

rows: Fetal period (flexed fetal position), kept for life
Early infancy, as the baby extends out of flexion

blocks.html: • Scoliosis = an abnormal sideways curve
2. A typical vertebra

• Body (front): carries weight, gets bigger going down
  • Arch (back) = pedicles (join arch to body) + laminae (close it behind)
    • vertebral foramen = the hole for the cord, between body and arch
    • spinous process (back) and transverse processes (sides) = muscle and ligament attachments
    • 4 articular processes → facet (zygapophyseal) joints = plane synovial joints between neighbours
  • The superior and inferior vertebral notches of neighbouring pedicles form the intervertebral foramen, where the spinal nerve exits

blocks.cap: Typical vertebra from above and from the side: body, pedicles, laminae, processes, vertebral foramen and intervertebral foramen

blocks.html: 3. The intervertebral disc

• Between vertebral bodies, joined to them at the end plate (cartilage fused to the disc + a thin layer of porous bone)
    • anulus fibrosus = outer rings of fibrocartilage
    • nucleus pulposus = inner gel, high water content
  • Strong attachment, allows movement, absorbs shock · about 25% of the column's height · thickest in cervical and lumbar spine · no disc between C1 and C2
4. Regional differences

rows: Short, with transverse foramina (vertebral artery C6 up to C1; only the vein at C7)
Long, with facets for the rib tubercle
Long and slender (Kai) · short and wide (medwiki) (sources differ - check the slides)
Long, slopes down over the next one
Rotation, some lateral flexion · facets and spines limit flexion and extension
Flexion, extension, some side bending, little rotation

blocks.html:
• Atypical cervical vertebrae
    • C1 (atlas): a ring - no body, no spinous process · lateral masses meet the occipital condyles → "yes" nod
    • C2 (axis): the dens projects up where C1's body would be → pivot joint → "no" rotation
5. Ligaments

rows: Broad, strong band on the front of bodies and discs, occiput to sacrum
Narrow, inside the canal on the back of the bodies
Tips of the spinous processes, C7 to sacrum
Continues the supraspinous above C7 to the skull · fills the neck curve
Attachment for neck and upper back muscles

blocks.cap: Ligaments of the vertebral column on a sagittal section, with the same ligaments on MRI

blocks.html: 6. Muscles of the back

rows: Elevates, depresses, retracts scapula · turns the glenoid up
Extends, adducts, medially rotates the humerus
Elevates scapula · turns the glenoid down
Retract scapula, turn the glenoid down, hold it to the chest wall
Erector spinae (iliocostalis lateral → longissimus → spinalis medial)
Both sides: extend spine and head, eccentrically control forward bending · one side: lateral flexion
Both: extend head and neck · one: lateral flexion + rotation
Rotation to the opposite side · stabilise · proprioception

blocks.html:
• Why they matter for back pain
    • erector spinae: strained lowering things to the floor (eccentric) or lifting them (concentric)
    • transversospinalis: rotates each segment, so over-rotation tears it - a frequent cause
    • neck: trapezius (people hold tension here), levator scapulae, splenius
  • Dorsal rami also become the skin nerves of the back and neck

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
lectures.title: Clinical approach to mechanical back and neck pain
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ No red flags and under 6 weeks → no imaging. Disc pain is worse with flexion; facet pain is worse with extension. Mechanical pain is worse with movement, better with rest, and never burning or tingling. Herniation = worse with cough or sneeze, sudden after lifting, younger patient. Whiplash: keep moving, no collar. Muscle pain is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Almost all back and neck pain is benign "mechanical" pain, and the work is to screen out the rare dangerous cause without over-investigating the common one. Ask about red flags every time; with none, an exact anatomical diagnosis is often unnecessary.
1. The approach

• Possible pain generators: paraspinal muscle and soft tissue · intervertebral disc · facet (zygapophyseal) joint · nerves in the spine · sacroiliac joint
  • History: a full pain history (OLD CARS: onset, location, duration, character, alleviating/aggravating, radiation, severity, or SOCRATES) plus red flags
  • Exam: the spine itself · contributing limb problems · a neurological exam · signs of red flags
    • palpable landmarks: C7 (vertebra prominens) · acromion · spine and medial border of the scapula · ribs 6-12 · iliac crest · sacrum
2. Red flags

rows: Progressive weakness or sensory change · saddle anesthesia · incontinence · erectile dysfunction · loss of hand dexterity · ataxic gait · abnormal reflexes
Morning stiffness · improves with exercise · pain in the 2nd half of the night · family history · rashes · eye symptoms
Young age · severe night pain, no relief with rest · weight loss · night sweats · history of cancer · associated signs (e.g. blood in the urine)
Fall or trauma · osteoporosis · previous fragility fracture
Dizziness with neck movement, cranial nerve signs, drop attacks · limb pain with activity (claudication)

blocks.html: 3. Investigations: when (not) to image

• Most low back pain needs no imaging
    • soft-tissue causes often don't show
    • can't separate symptomatic from asymptomatic changes - after a certain age everyone has them
    • it rarely changes management
  • Red flags → imaging is required, plus targeted tests (blood work and cultures for infection · other imaging for cancer · vascular imaging · electromyography for nerve problems)

rows: Cheap, quick screen of alignment and fractures
Best for non-bony structures · most expensive, longest wait
Disease in many places · "hot" vs "cold" lesions
Dye into the dural sac · only if MRI is contraindicated
Diagnosis and treatment (pain gone after a facet injection = facet was the source)

blocks.html: • After 6 weeks without red flags: an X-ray may be the starting point (medwiki) · X-ray only when looking for red-flag conditions, MRI preferred (Kai) (sources differ - check the slides)
4. Mechanical pain: what it looks like

• Definition: axial (spine) pain that is worse with movement and relieved by rest
    • site: midline or just beside it, neck or back
    • onset: anywhere from acute to chronic · usually built up by degeneration, then "tweaked" by stairs or a bad bend
    • character: dull ache or sharp, stabbing · not burning or tingling (that is nerve pain)
    • radiation: variable, but not to the tips of the limbs
    • red flags: none · imaging often normal
5. Muscle pain and whiplash

• Three muscle problems: acute strain or spasm · repetitive strain (repetition, force, vibration, compression, awkward postures) · myofascial trigger points (tender knots that give a reproducible referred pattern)
    • lumbar: erector spinae (strained lowering or lifting) · transversospinalis (rotation) · neck: trapezius, levator scapulae, splenius · sustained posture
  • No test proves it - a diagnosis of exclusion
  • Treatment (the template for most back pain): rule out red flags → reassure (common, benign, self-limiting, excellent prognosis) → relative rest, not bed rest → ice or heat → topical or a short course of oral anti-inflammatories → physiotherapy for postural support
  • Whiplash associated disorder: neck symptoms after an acceleration-deceleration injury (car crash)
    • muscles most often (strains, partial tears) · less often facets > bone > cord
    • under 5% still have severe symptoms at 2 years
    • X-ray if fracture is a worry · MRI if neurological signs · otherwise keep moving, no collar, heat or ice, acetaminophen or NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), modest physiotherapy (aggressive programs can worsen it)
6. Spondylosis: the degenerative cascade

• Spondylosis = spinal "arthritis" = degenerative disc disease + facet arthropathy with loss of disc height and thickened ligaments
  • The cascade: repeated axial loading → end-plate damage → tears in the anulus → nucleus pushes into the tears (internal disc disruption) → disc dries, flattens → angles change, lumbar curve lost → facets overloaded: synovial thickening, cartilage loss, osteophytes (bone spurs), lax capsule → slipping (degenerative spondylolisthesis) · thickened ligaments → less room for the nerves

rows: Nucleus pushes through tears in the anulus but stays inside it
Arthritis of the synovial facet joints
Imaging changes don't match symptoms (everyone gets them)
Localised, may be one-sided · refers: headache from the neck · buttock or leg from the lumbar spine, rarely past the knee
EXTENSION (bending back squeezes the facets) · eased by flexion
Flexion-based physiotherapy · NSAIDs, acetaminophen · facet injection · medial branch block or radiofrequency ablation (the medial branch supplies the facet)

blocks.alt: disc vs facet loading in flexion and extension - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Bending forward squeezes the disc; bending backward squeezes the facet joints
Referred pain maps from facet joints at each spinal level

blocks.html: 7. Disc herniation and spondylolisthesis

• Disc herniation: disc material goes beyond the anulus
    • causes both disc pain and nerve compression
    • younger patients · sudden pain after lifting · worse with coughing or sneezing
    • lumbar discs herniate posterolaterally, around the narrow posterior longitudinal ligament, towards the nerve roots
  • Degenerative spondylolisthesis: one vertebra slips on the next (usually forward) as spondylosis progresses

blocks.alt: disc bulge, protrusion, extrusion and sequestration - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: From normal disc to diffuse bulge, protrusion, extrusion and a free sequestered fragment

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord
lectures.title: Anatomy of the back and spinal cord
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The cord ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris) but the dural sac runs to S2 - so a lumbar puncture or epidural goes in at L3/L4 or L4/L5, into the cauda equina, not the cord. C1-C7 exit above their vertebra, C8 below C7, everything after below. Epidural space and subarachnoid space are real; subdural is potential. Ventral root = motor, dorsal root = sensory. C7 = middle finger, triceps · L5 = big toe extension · S1 = lateral foot, Achilles.

The spinal cord is shorter than the spine, and almost every clinical rule in this block follows from that: where it ends, which root a disc hits, where a needle can go safely, and why lumbar and cervical stenosis behave differently.
1. The spinal cord

• Part of the central nervous system, continuous with the medulla · a reflex centre and the pathway between body and brain
  • Runs from the foramen magnum to L1-L2 in adults
  • Not uniform in width
    • cervical enlargement (C4-T1 cord levels) → brachial plexus (upper limb)
    • lumbosacral enlargement (L1-S3 cord levels) → lumbar and sacral plexuses (lower limb)
  • The end of the cord
    • conus medullaris = the tapered tip, at L1-L2
    • filum terminale (internum) = a thread of pia from the tip to the coccyx, anchoring the cord
    • cauda equina ("horse's tail") = the lumbar and sacral roots running down past the cord's end to their own foramina
  • Why it is short: in the embryo the cord fills the canal, but the spine grows faster, leaving the cord in the upper two-thirds (Kai) · medwiki says the cord is at full adult length at birth and spans the whole column then (sources differ - check the slides)

blocks.alt: spinal cord enlargements and 31 pairs of spinal nerves - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The cord ends at L1-L2; cervical enlargement for the brachial plexus, lumbar enlargement for the lumbosacral plexus; 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal nerves

blocks.html: 2. Spinal nerves and where they exit
• 31 pairs: 8 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 sacral · 1 coccygeal

rows: Below C7 - there is no C8 vertebra
Leave the cord high, travel down as the cauda equina, exit at their own foramen
The gap between cord segment and foramen grows going down

blocks.html:
• Making a spinal nerve
    • ventral (anterior) rootlets = motor (+ presynaptic autonomic fibres) · dorsal (posterior) rootlets = sensory
    • rootlets → ventral and dorsal roots → join in the intervertebral foramen as a mixed spinal nerve
    • it splits into a dorsal ramus (skin and deep muscles of the back) and a ventral ramus (limbs and the rest of the trunk)
  • Review the inside of the cord in 04 - Introduction to the Nervous System
3. Meninges and spaces

rows: Real space outside the dura · fat + internal venous plexus
Tough outer layer · forms the dural sac down to S2 · anchored to the coccyx (filum terminale externum) · continuous with the cranial dura
Delicate, no blood vessels · held against the dura by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure
Real space with CSF and the cord's vessels · enlarges below the cord as the lumbar cistern (L2 to S2), holding the cauda equina
Directly on the cord, roots and vessels · denticulate ligaments anchor the cord to the dural sac · continues as the filum terminale

blocks.html: 4. Epidural vs spinal block and lumbar puncture

• Both done at L3/L4 or L4/L5 - below the end of the cord, so the floating cauda equina roots move away from the needle
  • Epidural: needle into the epidural space, around the dura · bathes the cauda equina roots as they leave the sac → numb below the level · widely used in labour
  • Spinal block / lumbar puncture: needle into the subarachnoid space · drug straight into CSF (onset ~5 minutes) or CSF sampled
    • patient on their side with the trunk flexed

blocks.cap: Epidural: needle stops in the epidural space; spinal block or lumbar puncture: needle enters the subarachnoid space and CSF

blocks.html: 5. Dermatomes, myotomes and root lesions

• Dermatome = skin supplied by one root · myotome = muscles supplied by one root
  • A root lesion gives sensory change in its dermatome, weakness in its myotome, and a reduced reflex
• C8 and L3 are in the objectives but neither source lists them - check the slides

blocks.cap: The cord tapers to the conus medullaris at L1-L2; the filum terminale anchors it; the cauda equina roots run on below

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
lectures.title: Clinical approach to non-mechanical back and neck pain
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Saddle anesthesia + urinary retention or fecal incontinence = cauda equina syndrome → urgent MRI and decompression within 48 hours. Lumbar stenosis squeezes roots (neurogenic claudication, eased by bending forward); cervical stenosis squeezes the cord (clumsy hands, upper motor neuron signs). A disc hits the lower root: C4/5 → C5, L4/5 → L5. Radicular pain is eased by slackening the nerve. Inflammatory pain gets better with movement. Spondylosis degenerates, spondylolysis fractures, spondylolisthesis slips.

Non-mechanical pain is either a squeezed nerve - at the side (radiculopathy) or in the centre (stenosis, myelopathy, cauda equina) - or "everything else" (inflammatory, fracture, visceral, infection, tumour). Without red flags, start the same conservative care as for mechanical pain.
1. Triage: which group is this?

blocks.html: • Nerve compression can come from anything that takes up space: disc, osteophyte, abscess, tumour, bleed, slipped vertebra
2. Radiculopathy: compression at the side

• Definition: a spinal nerve root compressed in or around the intervertebral foramen
    • degenerative causes are by far the most common (disc herniation, spondylosis)
    • others: trauma · tumour · infection · inflammation · cyst · osteoporotic fracture · sarcoidosis · diabetes · arteriovenous malformation
  • Presents as
    • limb > neck or back, in a dermatome
    • burning, tingling, electric (neuropathic) · can be very severe
    • eased by positions that slacken the nerve (arm overhead, legs curled)
    • weakness and reduced reflexes in a myotome · sensory change
  • Where: lumbar - over 99% degenerative, mostly L5 and S1 · cervical - mostly C7 and C6, from cervical spondylosis · thoracic herniation is rare
  • Which root does the disc hit? The lower one - for different reasons
    • cervical: nerves exit above their vertebra → C4/5 disc → C5
    • lumbar: the upper root has already left; a posterolateral disc hits the traversing root → L4/5 disc → L5 (a far-lateral disc can catch the exiting L4)

• Treatment
    • conservative first: education, excellent prognosis · relative rest, ice or heat · topicals, NSAIDs, short course of opioids if severe · physiotherapy
    • image if red flags, a non-degenerative cause is suspected, or the deficit is severe or progressing · electromyography shows how badly the nerve is affected
    • still failing → epidural steroid injection → surgical decompression (refractory pain, or a progressive or severe neurological deficit)

blocks.alt: which nerve root a lumbar vs cervical disc herniation hits - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: A paracentral L4/5 disc hits L5 while a far-lateral one hits L4; a C6/7 disc hits C7

blocks.html: 3. Central stenosis: lumbar roots vs cervical cord

• Spinal stenosis = a narrowed canal (disc, osteophyte, thickened ligament, tumour, degeneration)
  • No cord below L1 → lumbar stenosis squeezes roots, cervical stenosis squeezes the cord - so they behave and are treated differently

rows: Legs > back, both sides · burning, tingling · distal worse
Clumsy hands, wasted intrinsic hand muscles · arm tingling, distal worse · gait and balance problems · urinary incontinence (retention with overflow) · often a radiculopathy too
Neurogenic claudication: worse walking · relieved by bending forward ("shopping cart sign", walking uphill) and sitting (more slowly than vascular claudication)
Upper motor neuron signs below the level: spasticity, brisk reflexes, weakness
May have weakness or sensory change · no bladder or bowel problems
None, or non-urgent MRI (especially a surgical candidate)
Urgent neurosurgical or spine consult for decompression (unless very mild)

blocks.html: 4. Cauda equina syndrome

• The severe end of the lumbar stenosis spectrum: heavy compression of the lowest roots
  • Presents as: weakness · saddle anesthesia · urinary retention · fecal incontinence
  • Urgent MRI · a neurosurgical emergency - outcomes much better if decompressed within 48 hours of onset
  • See cauda equina syndrome
5. "Everything else"

rows: Night pain in the 2nd half of the night
Sacroiliac joints · ask about eyes, rashes, family history, enthesitis (inflamed tendon insertions), other joints

blocks.html:
• Inflammatory → seronegative spondyloarthropathies: ankylosing spondylitis · psoriatic arthritis · inflammatory bowel disease arthritis · reactive arthritis
  • Fractures
    • osteoporotic compression fracture: elderly, on steroids · minor or no trauma · axial pain ± radiation · treat the pain and the osteoporosis (e.g. bisphosphonates)
    • spondylolysis: fracture of the pars interarticularis (between pedicle and lamina) · young athletes who extend the back (gymnastics, football, weightlifting) · can lead to spondylolisthesis

rows: Slip of one vertebra on the next (degenerative, or from a spondylolysis)
Vascular: abdominal aortic aneurysm, vertebral artery insufficiency, atypical cardiac pain · GI: peptic ulcer, pancreatitis · genitourinary: pyelonephritis, kidney stones, endometriosis
Bone tumour · epidural or intradural mass · drop metastases · referred (e.g. renal cell, ovarian)
Young age, severe night pain, weight loss, night sweats, cancer history, blood in the urine

lectures.name: Axial Spine Radiology
lectures.title: Axial spine radiology
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Spondylolysis is seen on the oblique lumbar view as a collar on the Scottie dog; spondylolisthesis on the lateral as a step in the body corners. Odontoid view: C1's lateral masses must not overhang C2. Lateral cervical: four smooth lines. Absent pedicle on the AP = winking owl (lytic lesion). L5/S1 is normally narrower than L4/5 - don't call it disease.

Know what normal looks like on each view, then the one view and the one sign for each abnormality the objectives name: fracture, spondylolysis and scoliosis. Built from the medwiki X-ray notes this lecture note embeds; the upper-year notes have no radiology section.
1. When to X-ray the spine

• Lumbar: significant trauma · age under 20 or over 50 · history of cancer, ankylosing spondylitis or osteoporosis · long-term steroids · back pain over 6 weeks without improvement
  • Thoracic: fall from over 3 metres · ejection from a car or motorbike · neurological deficit · after surgery · chronic conditions · cancer history with back pain
  • Reading any view: vertebral bodies and spinous processes line up · disc spaces equal side to side and taller going down · body height steady or rising going down
2. Cervical spine

rows: Equal joint spaces · spinous processes midline and in line
Compression fracture · spinous process fracture of the lower neck (clay-shoveler) · disc herniation
C1's lateral masses must not overhang C2's
Dens fracture · C1 burst (Jefferson) fracture · transverse ligament injury · basilar invagination
The whole cervical spine · part of the trauma series (with chest and pelvis X-rays)
4 smooth lines: anterior vertebral · posterior vertebral · spinolaminar · posterior spinous
Compression, teardrop, hangman's, clay-shoveler fractures · facial, skull, airway injuries · osteoarthritis, spondylosis

blocks.html: 3. Thoracic spine

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Anatomy of the proximal upper extremity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Surgical neck fracture → axillary nerve · mid-shaft fracture → radial nerve (it lies in the radial groove). The glenohumeral joint trades stability for range - it is held by the labrum, rotator cuff and ligaments, and dislocates anteroinferiorly. The coracoacromial arch stops upward displacement, and the cuff tendons run underneath it (impingement). Sternoclavicular joint: the clavicle fractures before the joint dislocates. Supraglenoid = biceps, infraglenoid = triceps.

The bones and joints of the shoulder girdle and arm, learned for what goes wrong with them: which landmark breaks, which nerve runs beside it, and what holds each joint together. The muscles, nerves and vessels are next week.
1. The pectoral girdle and its four joints

• Pectoral girdle = clavicle + scapula, joining the arm to the trunk
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm: full shoulder movement needs the scapula to reposition the glenoid as the arm moves, giving the muscles a stable base

rows: Saddle synovial, works like a ball-and-socket · articular disc (shock absorber, stops medial dislocation)
Anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments · interclavicular · costoclavicular (limits elevation)
The only joint linking the arm to the axial skeleton · dislocation is rare - the clavicle breaks first · 1 ligament torn = subluxation · both = dislocation
Most mobile joint in the body · dislocation

blocks.html: • Which ligament carries the AC joint: the coracoclavicular, which suspends the scapula and arm from the clavicle (Kai) · the acromioclavicular, which gives most of the support (medwiki) (sources differ - check the slides)

blocks.html: 2. Clavicle and scapula

• Clavicle: S-shaped (medial half convex forward, lateral half concave) · enlarged triangular sternal end · flat acromial end
  • Scapula: triangular flat bone, essential for overhead movement

rows: Big attachment point for muscles and ligaments
Long head of biceps · long head of triceps
Splits the back into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae (homes of supraspinatus, infraspinatus)
Bridged by the transverse scapular ligament → a foramen for nerves and vessels

blocks.html: 3. Humerus and the elbow end

• Proximal humerus
    • head (meets the glenoid) · anatomical neck (just below the head)
    • greater (lateral) and lesser (front) tubercles = insertions · between them the intertubercular (bicipital) groove for the long head of biceps
    • surgical neck = the narrowing below the tubercles, a common fracture site
    • deltoid tuberosity (mid-shaft) · radial (spiral) groove on the back of the shaft for the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
  • Distal humerus
    • medial epicondyle: common flexor origin · ulnar nerve runs behind it
    • lateral epicondyle: common extensor origin
    • capitulum ↔ radial head (lateral) · trochlea ↔ trochlear notch of the ulna (medial)
    • coronoid fossa takes the ulna's coronoid process in full flexion · olecranon fossa takes the olecranon in full extension
  • Proximal forearm: radial head turns in the annular ligament · radial tuberosity (biceps) · olecranon (triceps) · coronoid process (brachialis)

rows: Surgical neck (low-energy fall onto the hand, elderly with osteoporosis)
Radial nerve + profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery

blocks.cap: Proximal humerus: head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles, intertubercular groove, deltoid tuberosity and radial groove

blocks.html: 4. The glenohumeral joint

• Built for mobility: large head in a shallow glenoid · lax capsule · bursae · lots of articular cartilage
  • Stabilisers
    • Glenoid labrum: fibrocartilage ring that deepens the socket
    • rotator cuff tendons: supraspinatus · infraspinatus · teres minor · subscapularis
    • ligaments

rows: Thickenings of the front of the capsule
Base of the coracoid → greater tubercle
Roof that stops the head moving up · so strong the humerus or clavicle breaks first
Holds the biceps tendon in its groove

blocks.html:
• The rotator cuff tendons pass under the arch · the gap narrows in full abduction
  • Bursae cut friction: subacromial (between acromion and cuff) · subscapular · Kai lists two, medwiki five (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Axillary recess: a loose pouch of the inferior capsule that allows the range
  • Blood supply: anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries · suprascapular artery · nerves (Hilton's law): suprascapular, axillary, pectoral, musculocutaneous, subscapular, radial
  • Clinically
    • dislocation is usually anterior and inferior (the arch blocks upward; the capsule is weakest in front and below) → axillary nerve at risk · treated with immobilisation, then rotator cuff strengthening
    • impingement: the supraspinatus tendon is pinched in the subacromial space · overuse stretches the static stabilisers → mild instability → cuff tires → secondary impingement

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the bones and joints of the shoulder
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Passive range of motion splits deep shoulder pain: lost in osteoarthritis and frozen shoulder (the X-ray tells them apart - osteophytes vs normal), preserved in inflammatory arthritis (with a weak cuff). Frozen shoulder: 20% of diabetics, normal X-ray. Traumatic instability is anterior and "torn loose" (surgery); atraumatic is multidirectional and "born loose" (physiotherapy). Posterior dislocation = seizure, alcohol, electrocution - missed on the AP view. AC arthritis: pain reaching across the chest, normal motion.

Two questions sort most of this lecture: is it the acromioclavicular (AC) joint or the glenohumeral joint, and is passive range of motion lost as well as active? Arthritis, instability and frozen shoulder each answer them differently. (Rotator cuff disease and biceps tendinopathy are in next week's notes.)
1. The approach
2. AC joint problems

• Common and easy to sort out · frequent in cyclists
  • AC joint arthritis (wear and tear)
    • history: localised, gradual, activity-related (reaching across the chest)
    • exam: small bump, tender, normal motion, weakness only from pain
    • X-ray: asymmetric joint space loss → bone on bone · osteophytes · subchondral cysts and sclerosis
    • treatment: education · activity modification (the main treatment) · ice, heat, steroid + local anesthetic injection · NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) · surgery last (resection arthroplasty)
  • AC joint separation
    • a force on the tip of the shoulder tears the acromioclavicular ± coracoclavicular ligaments · 40% of shoulder injuries, 10% of collision-sport injuries
    • presents as: pain, tenderness, a "piano key" shoulder

rows: Non-surgical: education, ice, NSAIDs, sling, early exercises
AC torn, coracoclavicular sprained - subluxation, clavicle slightly up
Clavicle severely elevated (by its own width) · deltoid and trapezius detached
Surgery for IV-VI (Kai) · medwiki names IV and V (sources differ - check the slides)

blocks.cap: Rockwood types I-VI of acromioclavicular joint injury, from a sprain to posterior, superior and inferior displacement

blocks.html: 3. Glenohumeral arthritis
• Progressive pain, lost range of motion, lost function · tell the types apart by passive range and cuff strength

rows: Asymmetric joint space · osteophytes · subchondral cysts, sclerosis
Methotrexate · hydroxychloroquine · anti-TNF (tumour necrosis factor) antibodies
Arthroscopic debridement (younger patients, not curative, eases catching) → standard (anatomic) arthroplasty

blocks.html:
• All: education · activity management · physiotherapy
  • Joint replacement: ~85% good outcome · complications: infection, loosening, instability, fracture, progressive disease

blocks.cap: X-rays of a normal shoulder, an anatomic (standard) replacement and a reverse replacement

blocks.html: 4. Instability

• Instability = the humeral head can't be kept centred in the glenoid · a spectrum: reduced → subluxed → dislocated
  • The ligaments and labrum matter most · they can tear or stretch · the labrum adds surface area and depth and acts as a bumper
  • Describe it by trauma, direction and degree

rows: "Born loose" - lax tissues, poor motor control
Reduction · surgery often (young or recurrent dislocators): labral repair, ~85% success
Physiotherapy and muscle control, not surgery · if needed, inferior capsular shift (~70%)

blocks.html:
• Direction of dislocation: anterior over 90% (blow to an abducted, externally rotated arm, or a fall on an outstretched hand) · posterior 2-4% (epilepsy, alcohol, electrocution) · inferior under 1% (arm stuck overhead)
  • Exam: apprehension and relocation test (anterior) · load and shift (anterior or posterior) · sulcus sign (inferior)
  • X-ray: at least 2 views to see the direction · posterior dislocation is easy to miss on the front-to-back (AP) view - get a scapular Y-view · repeat after reduction · associated Bankart lesion, Hill-Sachs lesion
5. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

• Adhesive capsulitis = global loss of active and passive motion with no other shoulder disorder found · cause unknown
    • 2% of adults · 20% of people with diabetes · usually in the 40s-50s
    • other links: thyroid disease, cardiac disease, cervical disc disease
  • Diagnosis of exclusion: X-ray is normal - use it and the trauma history to rule out arthritis, old fractures, heterotopic bone
  • Stages: freezing (inflamed, painful) → frozen (stiff, scarred capsule) → thawing
  • Treatment
    • education: self-limiting but slow (1-3 years) · 20-50% never fully lose pain or stiffness
    • pain relief (acetaminophen + ibuprofen)
    • physiotherapy is controversial - no good evidence, may inflame it early
    • intra-articular steroid in the freezing stage: better than physiotherapy early, no difference at 1 year · hydrodistension (saline under pressure to break the capsule)
    • surgery (capsulectomy): faster return of motion, same by 2 years

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus
lectures.title: Anatomy of the brachial plexus
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Superior trunk = C5 + C6, middle = C7, inferior = C8 + T1 - and the posterior cord takes all three posterior divisions, so the radial nerve, like the median, carries every root (C5-T1). Divisions give off no branches. Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior → winged scapula. Axillary nerve: deltoid + teres minor, at risk at the surgical neck and in dislocation. Radial nerve: at risk in the radial groove (mid-shaft fracture). The median and ulnar nerves pass through the arm but supply nothing there.

Five roots (C5-T1) regroup into five terminal nerves. The question the lecture turns on: from the muscles and skin that are lost, which part of the plexus is injured?
1. The five segments

• The brachial plexus = the ventral rami of C5-T1 (the cervical enlargement of the spinal cord) · starts in the neck, ends in the axilla as the terminal branches
  • In order: roots → trunks → divisions → cords → branches ("Really Thirsty? Drink Cold Beer")
  • The plexus "roots" are ventral rami, not the dorsal and ventral roots of a spinal nerve · each is already a mixed nerve (motor + sensory)

blocks.cap: The whole plexus: roots C5-T1, superior, middle and inferior trunks, anterior and posterior divisions, lateral, posterior and medial cords, and the five terminal branches with their roots

blocks.html: 2. Trunks, divisions and cords

• Trunks
    • superior = C5 + C6 · middle = C7 alone · inferior = C8 + T1
  • Divisions: each trunk splits into an anterior and a posterior division (6 in all)
    • no nerves branch off the divisions
    • anterior divisions → nerves to the flexor (front) compartments · posterior divisions → nerves to the extensor (back) compartments
  • Cords, named by where they sit around the axillary artery

rows: Anterior divisions of the superior + middle trunks
Anterior division of the inferior trunk, carrying on alone

blocks.html: 3. Branches before the terminal five

rows: Rhomboids · levator scapulae (pierces the middle scalene on the way back)
Pectoralis major and minor (pierces minor first)
Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm · of the forearm
Arm: T1 (medwiki figure) or C8-T2 (upper-year notes) - sources differ, check the slides · forearm: C8, T1
Skin only: medial arm · medial forearm

blocks.html: • The nerve to the subclavius also comes off at trunk level (the medwiki note: not examinable)
4. The five terminal branches

• The lateral and medial cords make an "M": musculocutaneous (lateral) · median (one root from each cord) · ulnar (medial)
  • The posterior cord ends as the axillary and the radial nerves
  • Count the roots: musculocutaneous 3 · axillary 2 · median 5 · radial 5 · ulnar 2

rows: Anterior arm: coracobrachialis (which it pierces), biceps, brachialis
Lateral forearm (as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm)
Most forearm flexors + 5 hand muscles · nothing in the arm
C8, T1 (upper-year notes: C7, C8, T1 - sources differ, check the slides)
Extensors of the back of the arm and forearm

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Muscles of the Shoulder
lectures.title: Anatomy of the muscles of the shoulder
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Supraspinatus starts abduction (the first 15°) and the deltoid takes over - and it is supraspinatus, squeezed under the coracoacromial arch, that wears out first. Infraspinatus and teres minor rotate laterally; subscapularis alone rotates medially and alone inserts on the lesser tubercle. Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior → winged scapula. Axillary nerve = deltoid + teres minor. Teres major is not in the cuff.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

Three groups of muscles move the shoulder: the pectoral muscles in front, the deltoid and teres major, and the four rotator cuff muscles that hold the humeral head in its socket. For each one, know where it attaches, which nerve supplies it and what it does.
1. Pectoral region

rows: Medial clavicle · sternum · upper 6 ribs and their costal cartilages
Lateral lip of the intertubercular groove
Adducts, flexes and medially rotates the humerus
Holds the scapula down and forward against the chest wall
Protracts the scapula (pushing, reaching: the "boxer's muscle") · keeps it flat on the chest wall

blocks.html:
• Pectoralis major is the most superficial muscle of the shoulder · pectoralis minor lies under it
  • Serratus anterior or its nerve damaged → winged scapula: the scapula lifts off the back of the chest wall when the patient pushes
2. Deltoid and teres major

rows: Lateral ⅓ of the clavicle · acromion · spine of the scapula
Anterior fibres: flex + medially rotate · middle fibres: abduct · posterior fibres: extend + laterally rotate
Medial lip of the intertubercular groove
Adducts + medially rotates the arm (one line of the upper-year notes says "abducts"; their slide and the medwiki say adducts)

blocks.html: • Teres major is not part of the rotator cuff · it sits below teres minor
3. Rotator cuff ("SITS")

rows: First 15° of abduction, then the deltoid takes over · no rotation

blocks.html:
• All four stabilise the glenohumeral joint - their main job - by holding the humeral head in the shallow socket during overhead movement
  • Three go to the greater tubercle; only subscapularis goes to the lesser tubercle
  • Roots: C5, C6 throughout the medwiki notes · the upper-year notes give subscapularis C5-C7 (sources differ - check the slides)
  • Supraspinatus runs under the coracoacromial ligament, above the humeral head: that space narrows when the arm is raised, so it is the tendon most prone to repetitive-motion damage - see 02.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder

blocks.cap: Rotator cuff from the front (subscapularis) and from behind (supraspinatus above the spine of the scapula, infraspinatus and teres minor below)
Insertions: supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor on the greater tubercle, subscapularis alone on the lesser tubercle

blocks.html: 4. Axillary artery

• Continues from the subclavian artery at the lateral border of the 1st rib · becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major
  • Split into 3 parts by pectoralis minor, which crosses in front of it

rows: Subscapular · anterior and posterior circumflex humeral

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the muscles of the shoulder
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Lost passive motion separates the stiff shoulders (degenerative arthritis, adhesive capsulitis) from rotator cuff disease, where active motion is worse than passive because of pain and weakness. Normal X-ray + global stiffness = adhesive capsulitis (think diabetes). Degenerative arthritis keeps cuff strength; inflammatory arthritis loses it. Traumatic instability is unidirectional and often needs surgery; atraumatic is multidirectional and gets physiotherapy. Anterior dislocation endangers the axillary nerve.

blocks.html: Built from upper-year notes and the medwiki note. Not yet checked against this year's lecture slides.

A painful shoulder: is it the AC joint, the rotator cuff, the glenohumeral joint itself, an unstable joint, or a frozen capsule? The biggest clue is whether passive movement is lost as well as active movement. (Biceps tendinopathy: see 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm.)
1. Acromioclavicular (AC) joint

• A plane synovial joint held by the AC ligament (on top) and the strong coracoclavicular ligament (conoid + trapezoid), which hangs the scapula and arm from the clavicle
  • AC joint arthritis (wear and tear)
    • History: localised pain, gradual onset, with activity (reaching across the chest)
    • Exam: small bump, tender, normal range of motion, weakness only from pain
    • X-ray: asymmetric joint space loss · osteophytes · cysts · subchondral sclerosis
    • Treatment: activity management · physical modalities · nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) · surgery
  • AC joint separation (injury)
    • upward force through the humerus → AC ligament tears (subluxation) · a blow to the tip of the shoulder → AC + coracoclavicular ligaments tear (dislocation): clavicle rides up, acromion stands out

rows: Subluxation: joint surfaces partly in contact

blocks.html: 2. Rotator cuff disease

• Definition: the most common shoulder disorder · rises with age, average onset in the 40s · progressive · 40% of older patients have it without symptoms
  • Causes
    • intrinsic (the main story): small vessels to the tendon disappear with age, starting on the articular side · tension overload breaks down collagen · tendon degeneration (less blood, collagen and water → brittle)
    • extrinsic: a smaller subacromial space · the acromion's shape was once blamed, but tears start on the articular side, not where the acromion rubs
    • overuse can also stretch the static stabilisers → mild instability → the cuff overworks and weakens → secondary impingement
  • Presents as: pain · weakness · restricted motion · painful arc between 40° and 120° of abduction
  • Exam
    • active motion less than passive (limited by pain)
    • impingement: Neer's test · Hawkins test · painful arc sign
    • strength: empty can test → supraspinatus · external rotation test → infraspinatus + teres minor · lift off test → subscapularis
  • Differential: shoulder bursitis · calcific tendinitis

rows: Full-thickness tear · humeral head rides up · joint fluid leaks out
Massive tear · humerus migrates up to the acromion · arthritis

blocks.html:
• Treatment: education · activity modification · NSAIDs · physiotherapy to recondition the muscles (the mainstay) · injection
    • surgery for persistent pain, weakness, or an acute tear

blocks.cap: Rotator cuff disease spectrum: impingement, partial-thickness tear, small and then massive full-thickness tear

blocks.html: 3. Glenohumeral arthritis
• Progressive pain, loss of range of motion and loss of function

rows: Asymmetric joint space loss · osteophytes · cysts · subchondral sclerosis
Symmetric joint space loss · deformity · erosions · osteopenia (washed-out bone)

blocks.html:
• Treatment: activity management · medication · physiotherapy · surgery
    • debridement: younger patients · removes damaged tissue for symptom relief, not curative
    • replacement: ~85% good outcome · risks: infection, loosening, instability, fracture, progressive disease
4. Instability

• Definition: the humeral head cannot be kept in the glenoid
  • Key structures: the glenohumeral ligaments (torn or stretched) and the labrum (deepens the socket, adds surface area, acts as a bumper) · lax tissue gives multidirectional instability
  • Describe it by trauma, direction and degree (subluxed vs dislocated)
  • Dislocation is usually forwards and downwards (the coracoacromial arch blocks upward escape; the capsule is weakest in front and below) → the axillary nerve is at risk
    • reduction: safety and monitoring · analgesia · manipulate to correct the deformity · recheck nerves and circulation afterwards

rows: Multidirectional, both sides, poor motor control · "born loose"
Reduce it · surgery often for the young or recurrent dislocator: labral repair (~85% success)
Physiotherapy and muscle control first · surgery: inferior capsular shift (~70%)

blocks.alt: glenohumeral joint reduced subluxated dislocated - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Degree of instability: reduced (head centred on the glenoid), subluxated (partly off), dislocated (fully off)

blocks.html: 5. Adhesive capsulitis ("frozen shoulder")

• Adhesive capsulitis: 2% of adults, 20% of people with diabetes, usually in their 40s-50s · cause unknown
  • Presents as: spontaneous onset · global loss of both active and passive motion
  • A diagnosis of exclusion: rule out intra-articular causes (arthritis, post-traumatic deformity) and extra-articular ones (capsular, muscular, heterotopic bone) with an X-ray and a trauma history
  • Associations: diabetes · weaker links with cervical disc disease, thyroid disease, cardiac disease · mostly idiopathic
  • Stages: freezing → frozen → thawing
  • Treatment: education, pain control, physiotherapy (evidence is weak)
    • intra-articular steroid beats physiotherapy early, but no difference at 1 year · hydrodistension (stretching the capsule open with fluid under pressure)
    • surgery: motion returns faster, same result at 2 years

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Muscles of the Arm
lectures.title: Anatomy of the muscles of the arm
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The biceps' main job is supination; brachialis, not biceps, is the primary elbow flexor. Musculocutaneous = everything in front; radial = triceps behind. Biceps long head starts on the supraglenoid tubercle, triceps long head on the infraglenoid tubercle - both cross the shoulder. Coracobrachialis crosses only the shoulder; brachialis only the elbow. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis.

The arm (shoulder to elbow) is two compartments, each with one job and one nerve: the front flexes, the back extends. The detail worth knowing is which joints each muscle crosses, because that decides what it can move.
1. Two compartments
• Under the skin, the brachial fascia wraps the arm · the medial and lateral intermuscular septa run from it to the humerus and divide the arm into front and back

rows: Flex the shoulder · flex the elbow · supinate the forearm

blocks.cap: Cross-section of the arm: biceps and brachialis in front (musculocutaneous nerve), the three heads of triceps behind (radial nerve), split by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa

blocks.html: 2. Anterior compartment

rows: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle, then through the intertubercular groove · short head: coracoid process
Supination - its main job · elbow flexion · weak shoulder flexion · resists shoulder dislocation
Middle ⅓ of the medial humerus
Flexes and adducts the shoulder · resists dislocation
Distal ½ of the anterior humerus

blocks.html:
• Biceps is the most superficial · coracobrachialis and brachialis lie deep to it
  • The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, which makes the muscle easy to find, then runs between biceps and brachialis
  • Musculocutaneous roots: C5-C7
3. Posterior compartment

rows: Proximal ⅓ of the posterior humerus, above the radial groove
Distal ⅓ of the posterior humerus, below the radial groove

blocks.html:
• All three heads share one tendon onto the olecranon of the ulna
  • Actions: primary elbow extensor · the long head also extends the shoulder and resists dislocation
  • Nerve: radial (C5-T1), which runs in the radial groove between the lateral and medial heads' origins

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the muscles of the arm
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Tenderness in the intertubercular groove, with pain on resisted shoulder and elbow flexion, points to the long head of biceps; weakness plus a retracted-muscle bulge means it has torn. The exam is the most useful test - ultrasound if unclear, MR arthrogram if you suspect a SLAP lesion. The tendon heals poorly (little blood supply), and most cases settle with active physiotherapy.

Deep pain at the front of the shoulder: is it the long head of the biceps tendon, or something next to it? The tendon shares its space with the rotator cuff and its origin with the labrum, so the exam and the differential do most of the work. (The other shoulder conditions in this lecture's objectives are charted in 02.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder.)
1. Proximal biceps tendinopathy

• Proximal biceps tendinopathy = a common cause of shoulder pain
  • "Tendinopathy", not "tendinitis": it covers the whole range from overuse and degeneration (tendinosis) to acute inflammation to tears
  • Who
    • younger: overhead-throwing athletes · inflammatory conditions (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis)
    • older: overuse and degeneration
2. Why the long head is vulnerable

• Next to the rotator cuff tendons → shares their wear and impingement
  • Runs through the tight intertubercular groove → easily irritated
  • Starts on the supraglenoid tubercle and the superior glenoid labrum → labrum problems (e.g. a tear) often drag the biceps in
  • The proximal tendon is relatively short of blood supply → heals poorly

blocks.cap: The long head of biceps tendon runs over the humeral head beside the rotator cuff tendon and attaches at the top of the glenoid

blocks.html: 3. History and exam

• History: acute or chronic · deep anterior shoulder pain
  • Exam (the most helpful step)
    • tender over the tendon in the intertubercular groove
    • pain worse with shoulder flexion and elbow flexion, with the forearm supinated
    • Speed's test · Yergason's test
    • a tear → weakness (especially supination) and a visible bulge as the muscle retracts (the "Popeye" deformity)

blocks.html: 4. Differential diagnosis

• Neighbouring tendon or bursa: rotator cuff tendinopathy · subacromial bursitis
  • Joint: SLAP lesion (a tear of the superior labrum, front to back) · shoulder arthritis · AC joint arthritis
  • Referred pain: cervical radiculopathy · facet joint arthropathy · visceral pain felt in the shoulder
5. Management

• Education: prognosis depends on the cause · most cases are chronic degeneration or overuse and improve with conservative care
  • Conservative
    • physiotherapy - active therapy is needed to improve
    • relative rest (avoid overhead activity)
    • nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) as needed · steroid injection
  • Surgery for refractory cases
    • the tendon is usually too degenerate to repair, so it is released and reattached lower down to control symptoms

lectures.name: Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Neurovascular supply of the proximal upper extremity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The radial nerve and profunda brachii lie together in the radial groove, so a mid-shaft humerus fracture threatens both; the axillary nerve goes with a surgical neck fracture, the ulnar nerve with the medial epicondyle. Median and ulnar nerves supply nothing in the arm. Axillary → brachial at the lower border of teres major; brachial → radial + ulnar in the cubital fossa. Median cubital vein = blood draws.

Follow the main artery from the neck to the elbow, then the five nerves that run beside it. The clinical payoff is which nerve or vessel a fracture at each level of the humerus puts at risk.
1. Arteries

• Subclavian artery: from the brachiocephalic trunk on the right, straight off the aortic arch on the left · two branches matter for the limb
    • dorsal scapular → upper superficial back muscles
    • suprascapular → back of the shoulder · runs with the suprascapular nerve, above the transverse scapular ligament
  • Axillary artery: from the lateral border of the 1st rib to the lower border of teres major · 3 parts, set by pectoralis minor in front of it

Thoracoacromial → acromial, pectoral, clavicular, deltoid regions · lateral thoracic → lateral chest wall, pectoral region, breast

Subscapular → thoracodorsal (superficial back) + circumflex scapular (triangular space) · anterior circumflex humeral · posterior circumflex humeral (with the axillary nerve, quadrangular space) - the two circle the surgical neck

• Brachial artery: runs medial to biceps, in front of coracobrachialis and brachialis · ends in the cubital fossa as the radial (lateral) and ulnar (medial) arteries
    • profunda brachii (deep brachial) → posterior compartment, in the radial groove with the radial nerve · becomes the radial collateral artery at the elbow
    • superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries → the network around the elbow
    • blood pressure: the cuff compresses the brachial artery; listen over it in the cubital fossa

blocks.html: 2. Veins

• Deep veins travel in pairs with the arteries
  • Superficial veins
    • cephalic vein: up the front and outer (lateral) forearm and arm → the end of the axillary vein
    • basilic vein: up the inner (medial) forearm and lower arm → joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein
    • median cubital vein: crosses the cubital fossa between them → the usual vein for blood draws and IV access
3. Nerves of the arm

• The ulnar nerve can be hard to pick out: the medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm run beside it, but they are smaller and branch off higher up

lectures.name: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Osteology of the distal upper extremity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Scaphoid = the most fractured carpal bone; lunate = the most dislocated, and it can press on the median nerve in the carpal tunnel. Capitulum ↔ radial head, trochlea ↔ trochlear notch. Carrying angle over 15° = valgus, under 5° = varus. Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are pivots; the middle one is a syndesmosis. The thumb's saddle CMC joint is what lets it oppose. Colles = distal 2 cm of the radius after a fall on the outstretched hand.

From the elbow to the fingertips: which bump fits into which socket, and what each joint lets you do. The landmarks matter because they are what you name on a plain X-ray and where the tendons and nerves attach.
1. Bones of the elbow and forearm

rows: Common flexor origin · ulnar nerve runs behind it
Meets the trochlear notch of the ulna

blocks.html: 2. Elbow joint

• Elbow = a synovial hinge (flexion and extension only) with two articulations
    • humeroulnar (trochlea + trochlear notch) = the main hinge
    • humeroradial (capitulum + radial head)
  • Capsule weak in front and behind (to allow flexion and extension), reinforced at the sides by the collateral ligaments
    • radial collateral ligament: lateral epicondyle → blends into the annular ligament
    • ulnar collateral ligament: medial epicondyle → the ulna (coronoid process and olecranon in the upper-year notes; "distal end of the ulna" in the medwiki - sources differ, check the slides) · 3 bands: anterior (cord-like, strongest) · posterior (fan-like, weakest) · oblique (deepens the socket of the trochlear notch)
  • Subcutaneous olecranon bursa: between the skin and the olecranon, stops friction · inflamed = olecranon bursitis, one of the most common bursitis sites
  • Carrying angle (arms at the sides, palms forward): normally 5-15° away from the body
    • over 15° = cubitus valgus · under 5° = cubitus varus · asymmetry between sides can signal disease
    • a little valgus is normal and more common in females

blocks.cap: Medial elbow: the ulnar collateral ligament with its anterior, posterior and oblique bands, and the annular ligament round the radial head

blocks.html: 3. Radioulnar joints (pronation and supination)

rows: Radial head + radial notch of the ulna
Ulnar head + ulnar notch of the radius
Triangular articular disc (clinicians: triangular fibrocartilage complex, TFCC)

blocks.html: • Pronation: the distal radius swings forwards and medially, crossing over the ulna · supination uncrosses it
4. Wrist: the carpal bones

• Lateral → medial, proximal row first: "Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle"
    • proximal row: scaphoid · lunate · triquetrum · pisiform
    • distal row: trapezium ("trapezium at the thumb") · trapezoid · capitate · hamate (with a hook)
  • Scaphoid = the most commonly fractured carpal bone (scaphoid fracture)
  • Lunate = the most commonly dislocated (still uncommon) · can compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
  • Pisiform + hook of the hamate form the ulnar canal

blocks.cap: Carpal bones from the front: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform in the proximal row; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate with its hook in the distal row

blocks.html: 5. Hand

• Metacarpals: 5, each with a base, shaft and head
  • Phalanges: thumb 2 (no middle phalanx), other digits 3 · proximal largest, distal smallest · the thumb also has 2 sesamoid bones
  • Digits are numbered 1-5 from lateral (thumb) to medial, and also have clinical names

rows: 2 and 3 barely move · 4 a little · 5 moderately (flexes and rotates in a tight grip)
Every plane - flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction · makes opposition possible
Digits 2-5: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction · thumb: flexion and extension only

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Elbow
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the elbow
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A young child who will not use an arm after it was pulled has a radial head subluxation: reduce it by pronation and extension, no cast needed. An adult elbow dislocation after a FOOSH is an emergency: check the ulnar nerve and watch for compartment syndrome. A red, warm olecranon swelling is infection until proven otherwise, so aspirate it. Valgus laxity with medial pain in a thrower = ulnar collateral ligament.

Elbow pain is sorted two ways: by where it hurts (front, inside, outside, back) and by which tissue is at fault (bone and joint, tendon, or something else). Joint and ligament problems cost range of motion and stability. A fracture can sit anywhere, so keep it on every list.
1. The differential, by location

• The upper-year list is longer
    • anterior: anterior capsule strain · loose body in the joint · pronator syndrome
    • medial: valgus extension overload syndrome
    • lateral: osteochondral defect · plica · posterolateral rotatory instability · radial tunnel (posterior interosseous nerve) syndrome
    • posterior: olecranon stress fracture · posterior impingement · gout

blocks.html: 2. Arthritis of the elbow

• Types
    • inflammatory: rheumatoid arthritis · psoriatic arthritis · gout · infection
    • non-inflammatory: degenerative (slow, gradual) · post-traumatic (osteoarthritis earlier, possibly in a different pattern)
  • Presents as: dull, achy pain with flares · stiffness · lost range of motion · locking
  • X-ray: uneven loss of joint space · osteophytes (bony spurs) · subchondral cysts · subchondral sclerosis
  • Treatment
    • education: a long, "grumbling" course with no cure
    • ice or heat · oral or topical anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs; upper-year notes add acetaminophen) · steroid injection into the joint
    • physiotherapy to keep range of motion · occupational therapy to keep function
    • surgery only when intolerable or not settling: arthroscopic debridement or joint replacement (arthroplasty)

blocks.html: 3. Dislocations: two joints, two different patients

rows: Proximal radioulnar: the radial head slips out of the annular ligament
Fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) · car crash, bracing against the dashboard
Child, rare after age 5, girls and left arm more often · a pull along the arm
Uncommon, because the trochlea sits securely in the trochlear notch · posterior is most common

Severe pain, worse with movement · lost range of motion
Child will not use the arm and holds it flexed against the body
Clinical diagnosis · X-ray only to rule out a fracture
Closed reduction + splint at 90° (may fail if soft tissue is trapped) · otherwise open reduction internal fixation
Closed reduction by pronation and extension · no cast or splint

blocks.html:
• Elbow dislocation is an emergency: capsule rupture · torn ligaments · broken skin · nerve injury, especially the ulnar nerve · compartment syndrome
  • The medwiki note calls the child's injury a radial head dislocation; upper-year notes call it a subluxation

blocks.cap: Elbow dislocations by direction: posterior (the most common), anterior, lateral, medial and divergent

blocks.html: 4. Ulnar collateral ligament injury

• The ligament is the main stabiliser of the medial elbow · injured by chronic, repetitive overuse (baseball pitchers)
  • Presents as: medial elbow pain, tender on palpation · a sudden pop if it tears acutely · too much valgus movement, with no firm end point on valgus stress
  • Investigations: valgus stress test · likely needs an exam by sports medicine or orthopaedics · MRI for the soft tissue
  • Treatment
    • education: ligaments heal slowly, if at all
    • ice · topical or oral anti-inflammatories · physiotherapy for the muscles that stabilise the elbow · brace
    • reconstruction only when needed for functional goals (professional athletes), with long physiotherapy after
5. Olecranon bursitis

• A bursa is a flat, fluid-filled sac that lets tissue glide over bone; irritated, it fills with fluid · the olecranon bursa is the most common superficial bursitis
  • Causes: one hard blow (a fall on the elbow) · repeated leaning (some jobs) · infection (look for a break in the skin)
  • Rule out infectious bursitis: redness, warmth, fever → aspirate the joint · drain and give antibiotics
  • Not every swollen elbow is bursitis: gout and rheumatoid arthritis can look the same and need their own treatment
  • Investigations: usually none · X-ray after trauma · aspirate if infection is suspected · ultrasound or MRI if atypical (upper-year notes)
  • Treatment: benign and self-limiting once the cause stops · rest, ice, compression, elevation · pad the elbow, stop leaning on it · topical or oral anti-inflammatories · bursectomy for a chronic case (upper-year notes also list an infected one)

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Anatomy of the muscles of the distal upper extremity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Flexor carpi ulnaris and the half of flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers are the 1½ anterior forearm muscles on the ulnar nerve; every other anterior muscle is median, and every posterior muscle is radial. Flexor digitorum profundus is the only muscle that bends the fingertip. Brachioradialis sits in the back but flexes the elbow. Palmaris longus is missing in 15% of people. Mallet finger = splint the tip straight for 6-8 weeks.

The forearm is two compartments with two nerves and two epicondyles: the front flexes and pronates, runs on the median nerve and starts at the medial epicondyle; the back extends and supinates, runs on the radial nerve and starts at the lateral epicondyle. The exceptions are what gets examined.
1. Compartments of the forearm

• The forearm runs from the cubital fossa to the wrist · radius laterally, ulna medially, joined by the interosseous membrane
  • The bones, the membrane and the anterior intermuscular septum, inside the antebrachial fascia, split it into two compartments
  • They are named "anterior" and "posterior" for where their muscles attach, although they sit more medially and laterally

blocks.html:
• Upper-year notes add anconeus (lateral epicondyle to olecranon): weak elbow extension, steadies the elbow
  • Brachioradialis is a posterior muscle that behaves like an anterior one
  • Extensor expansion: a flat, triangular hood of tendon over the back of each finger; extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor indicis, the lumbricals and the interossei all insert into it
  • Wrist side-to-side movement takes a flexor and an extensor together: radial deviation = flexor carpi radialis + both radial extensors · ulnar deviation = flexor carpi ulnaris + extensor carpi ulnaris
4. Clinical relevance

• Anatomical snuffbox: the hollow at the base of the thumb when it is extended
    • borders: abductor pollicis longus + extensor pollicis brevis on one side, extensor pollicis longus on the other (sources differ: this note names the extensor pollicis longus and brevis as its borders, the 07.1 note names the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis - check the slides)
    • floor: scaphoid and trapezium · the radial artery runs in it and its pulse can be felt there
  • Ganglion cyst: a lump filled with synovial fluid over a joint or tendon of the hand or wrist, most often the back of the wrist
    • no treatment needed · drain or excise only if bothersome (risk of infection) · the old "bible bump" smash is no longer advised
  • Mallet finger: the extensor tendon tears off at the fingertip joint, often when a ball strikes the straight finger and bends the tip
    • the fingertip droops and cannot be straightened
    • splint the fingertip joint straight for 6-8 weeks · surgery to pin it if a bone fragment came off (upper-year notes)

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the muscles of the distal upper extremity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Most elbow tendon pain is tendinosis: degeneration without inflammation, treated with eccentric physiotherapy for 12 weeks rather than anti-inflammatories alone. Tennis elbow = extensor carpi radialis brevis, pain just below the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist extension and gripping. Golfer's elbow = flexor-pronator origin, pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation. A distal biceps rupture (pop, bruise, Popeye bulge, weak supination) must be repaired within 6-10 days. Tendon problems do not reduce range of motion; joint problems do.

Tendon problems around the elbow cause pain and pain-related weakness but do not take away range of motion. Most are a slow, degenerative tendinosis rather than an inflamed tendinitis, which is why rest and anti-inflammatories alone rarely fix them.
1. Tendinitis vs tendinosis

rows: Collagen degeneration, no inflammation · the tendon turns dull, brownish and soft · immature, disorganised collagen (type III in place of type I) with a poor blood-vessel response
Acute injury or overload · rheumatologic disease · infection
Chronic overuse with too little recovery time
Reduce inflammation: rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE) · anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs) · treat the cause
Pain relief · physiotherapy to build new collagen · anti-inflammatories have little to act on
Fast, once the cause is dealt with

blocks.html: 2. Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow)

• What it is: degeneration of the common extensor tendon origin, usually extensor carpi radialis brevis
    • the old name "epicondylitis" implies inflammation; there usually is none (sources differ: one upper-year anatomy note still describes it as inflammation of the epicondyle, while the medwiki note and the upper-year clinical note call it degeneration - check the slides)
  • Who: 1-3% of people (a year, in upper-year notes) · 30s and 40s · mostly work overuse, not sport
  • Presents as: pain just below the lateral epicondyle, not on it · pain and weakness with gripping and supination
  • Exam
    • tender over the common extensor tendon
    • pain on resisted wrist extension and on resisted extension of the middle finger
    • pain on passive wrist flexion (stretching the extensors)
  • Investigations: probably none at first
  • Memory hook: TENnis = exTENsor · "tennis" has no L, so add one: Lateral
3. Medial epicondylosis (golfer's elbow)

• What it is: degeneration of the flexor-pronator common origin at the medial epicondyle, from overuse (the golf swing loads it)
  • Presents as: pain just below the medial epicondyle, tender there · pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation · pain on passive wrist extension
  • Memory hook: goLFEr = FLExor · "golf" already has its L, so Medial

blocks.html: 4. Distal biceps tendinopathy and rupture

rows: Acute, after trauma or at the end of long overuse
Anterior elbow pain on resistance and on stretch
A pop, heard or felt · pain (or none) · bruising (tendons bleed) · weak supination, weaker flexion · change in the muscle's shape (a "Popeye" bulge)
Orthopaedics: repair is very fixable within 6-10 days, not later

blocks.html:
• Upper-year notes compare the three biceps ruptures
    • proximal long head: not uncommon · arm still works because of the short head · surgery rarely needed
    • proximal short head: rarely ruptures
    • distal: rare but consequential, so it is the one to repair
5. Treating any tendinopathy

• Education: expectations, restrictions, timelines · many settle quickly, some become chronic
  • Relative rest: gentler use, breaks or task switching · fix ergonomics and technique
  • Splints, braces or taping to support and redirect force
  • Ice (upper-year notes: 20 minutes on, 20 off, to calm abnormal new blood vessels)
  • Physiotherapy: eccentric strengthening twice a day for 12 weeks, to lay down and align new collagen
  • Massage, which may stimulate fibroblasts to make collagen
  • Drugs: oral, topical or injected anti-inflammatories, which may do little in a chronic tendinosis · platelet-rich plasma is uncertain
  • Surgery: orthopaedics if the tendon has ruptured

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Anatomy of the neurovascular supply of the distal upper extremity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Cubital fossa, lateral to medial = biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, median Nerve (TAN), with the median cubital vein on top for blood draws. The ulnar nerve is exposed behind the medial epicondyle; the median nerve is pinched at pronator teres and the carpal tunnel. The radial pulse sits beside flexor carpi radialis and in the snuffbox. C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger. T1 = spreading and closing the fingers.

Know where each forearm nerve can be pinched, where to feel a pulse and draw blood, and which spinal root a movement or patch of skin tests. The cubital fossa is where most of it meets.
1. Arteries of the forearm
• The brachial artery splits in the cubital fossa into the radial artery (lateral) and the ulnar artery (medial)

rows: Lateral forearm beside the radial nerve, deep to brachioradialis · at the wrist it wraps round the radius onto the back, across the anatomical snuffbox and over the scaphoid
Radial recurrent (joins the network round the elbow)
Radial pulse: at the wrist between the flexor carpi radialis and abductor pollicis longus tendons, and in the snuffbox
Medial forearm beside the ulnar nerve, deep to pronator teres · enters the wrist beside the pisiform
Anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent (elbow network) · common interosseous → anterior interosseous (with the anterior interosseous nerve) and posterior interosseous

blocks.html: • Collateral network round the elbow (recurrent and collateral arteries joining up): if the brachial artery is blocked or clamped below the deep artery of the arm, the forearm still gets blood
2. Veins of the forearm

• Superficial veins start in the dorsal venous network on the back of the hand
    • Cephalic (lateral): up the arm, through the groove between deltoid and pectoralis major, into the axillary vein (sources differ: the medwiki note says it drains into the axillary artery, upper-year notes say the axillary vein - check the slides)
    • Basilic (medial): partway up the arm, then dives deep to join the brachial veins and form the axillary vein
    • Median cubital: crosses the cubital fossa joining cephalic to basilic
  • Deep veins run in pairs with the arteries (radial, ulnar, brachial) · perforating veins shunt blood from the superficial veins to the deep ones

blocks.cap: Arteries and veins of the arm: radial and ulnar arteries from the brachial, the cephalic vein laterally, the basilic vein medially, and the median cubital vein joining them at the elbow

blocks.html: 3. Cubital fossa

• A triangle on the front of the elbow: brachioradialis (lateral) · pronator teres (medial) · a line between the two epicondyles (top)
  • Contents, lateral to medial ("TAN"): biceps Tendon · brachial Artery · median Nerve
    • upper-year notes also place the radial nerve (with its deep and superficial branches) at the lateral edge
  • Superficial: median cubital, cephalic and basilic veins · medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm
  • Clinically: median cubital vein = blood draws and IV lines · brachial artery = where blood pressure is measured

blocks.html: 4. Nerves of the forearm

rows: Through the cubital fossa (superficial here), between the two heads of pronator teres, between the two finger flexors, then under the flexor retinaculum

lectures.title: Clinical approach to the neurovascular supply of the distal upper extremity
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow = medial elbow pain, tingling in the ring and little fingers and a positive Tinel sign at the elbow; treat first by stopping pressure on the elbow and night-time bending, and operate only for severe or progressive weakness. Weakness without pain is uncommon and narrows the differential. True sensory loss means a nerve problem. An ulnar lesion at the elbow weakens fingertip flexion of the ring and little fingers; one in Guyon's canal does not. Pronator syndrome numbs the palm too; carpal tunnel syndrome spares its centre.
