With a nerve complaint at the elbow, first ask whether it is weakness, pain or both, and whether the numbness is a true loss of sensation. Then find the site: the commonest is the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
1. Weakness and abnormal sensation around the elbow

• Weakness is a very common complaint when there is pain
    • first question: is it weakness, pain, or both? · pain without weakness is common · pain with weakness is common · weakness without pain is uncommon, which narrows the list
    • second question: if the weakness is real, what is causing it?
  • Abnormal sensation
    • a nerve injury can give too much feeling (tingling, spontaneous pain) and too little (numbness) at the same time
    • tingling or pain can come from nerve, muscle, tendon, ligament, bone or joint, or be referred from elsewhere
    • true sensory loss is neurogenic: it comes from the peripheral or central nervous system
2. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome)

• What it is: the ulnar nerve squeezed or irritated where it runs behind the medial epicondyle
  • Causes
    • direct trauma (hitting the "funny bone") · repeated pressure (leaning on a desk)
    • long periods with the elbow bent stretch the nerve (during sleep)
    • the nerve slipping over the epicondyle as the elbow bends · thickened ligament · medial epicondylosis
  • Presents as
    • medial elbow pain
    • numbness and tingling in the ring and little fingers ("they fall asleep")
    • weakness of the hand, because the ulnar nerve drives the interossei · lower motor neuron weakness only in muscles the ulnar nerve supplies below the elbow
    • medial forearm skin: spared in the medwiki note, because a branch of the medial cord supplies it (sources differ: upper-year notes describe numbness running from the medial forearm into the ring and little fingers - check the slides)
  • Exam: Tinel sign positive at the elbow (tapping over the nerve sends tingling down its territory) · map sensory loss · test the hand muscles · the nerve may slip on bending
  • Investigations
    • electromyography (EMG) or a nerve conduction study separates irritation from real nerve damage · needed sooner if weakness is significant or getting worse
    • nerve ultrasound or MRI · X-ray if elbow arthritis or an old injury is suspected (upper-year notes)
  • Treatment
    • education matters most: irritation (neuritis) is fully reversible, and so is mild nerve damage, because peripheral nerves regrow
    • avoid pressure on the elbow (pad it, change the workstation)
    • avoid bending the elbow fully at night: a towel splint or elbow pad
    • medication is neither needed nor helpful
    • surgery for severe or progressive cases: ulnar neurolysis (freeing it from scar) or transposition (moving it out from behind the epicondyle)

• What it is: the median nerve squeezed between the two heads of pronator teres, usually from muscle bulk built by elbow overuse
  • Presents as: pain and tenderness at the top of the front of the forearm · altered sensation over the palm side of the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger, and the adjoining palm
  • Upper-year notes contrast it with carpal tunnel syndrome, which spares a patch of central palm because that skin's nerve branch leaves before the tunnel

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 1
lectures.title: Anatomy of the wrist and hand, part 1
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The carpal tunnel is carpal bones roofed by the flexor retinaculum, and it carries nine tendons (4 superficialis, 4 profundus, flexor pollicis longus) plus the median nerve; the ulnar nerve and artery run outside it. The thumb's CMC joint is a saddle, which is what lets the thumb oppose. Thenar muscles = recurrent branch of the median nerve; nearly every other intrinsic muscle = deep branch of the ulnar. PAD and DAB: palmar interossei adduct, dorsal interossei abduct. Superficial arch = mostly ulnar; deep arch = mostly radial.

Part 1 builds the hand from the inside out: the joints and what each one allows, the fascial bands that hold the tendons down and roof the carpal tunnel, the five muscle compartments with their nerves, and the two arterial arches. The nerves of the hand are Part 2.
1. Joints of the wrist and hand
• All are synovial: a capsule lined by synovial membrane that makes lubricating fluid

blocks.html: 2. Fascia of the wrist and hand

• Palmar aponeurosis: where palmaris longus inserts · longitudinal fibres fan from the flexor retinaculum to the four fingers and blend with their tendon sheaths · its septa divide the palm into compartments
    • upper-year notes: in Dupuytren's contracture it thickens and scars, pulling fingers into fixed flexion; the diseased tissue has to be cut out
  • Palmar carpal ligament: a thickening of the forearm fascia, continuous with the extensor retinaculum on the back · superficial and proximal to the flexor retinaculum
  • Flexor retinaculum: deeper · the roof of the carpal tunnel · spans scaphoid and trapezium (lateral) to pisiform and hook of the hamate (medial)
  • Carpal tunnel: carpal bones for a floor, flexor retinaculum for a roof
    • inside: 4 flexor digitorum superficialis tendons · 4 flexor digitorum profundus tendons · flexor pollicis longus · the median nerve
    • outside, on top of the retinaculum: the ulnar nerve and artery · the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve · palmaris longus tendon
  • Fibrous digital sheaths (flexor pulleys): tunnels of fibrous tissue binding the flexor tendons to each finger's bones · work as pulleys and stop the tendons bowstringing
  • Synovial sheaths: fluid-filled sleeves inside the fibrous sheaths that let the tendons glide
    • upper-year notes: an infected sheath (tenosynovitis) gives a swollen finger that hurts to move; usually it stays in that finger but can spread into the palm and forearm

lectures.title: Clinical approach to the wrist and hand, part 1
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH with a normal X-ray is treated as a scaphoid fracture anyway: blood reaches the scaphoid from its far end, so a missed fracture can end in non-union or osteonecrosis. Distal radius X-ray = short (ulnar variance), crooked (volar tilt), smooth (step over 1 mm needs fixing). Make the deformity worse to unlock it, then reduce and cast with a 3-point mould. Treatment is forgiving at the extremes of age; middle-aged, active patients need the most. Tingling in the thumb and first two fingers after a wrist fracture = acute carpal tunnel syndrome.

Two fractures from a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH): the distal radius, judged on X-ray by three questions (is it short? crooked? smooth?), and the scaphoid, which can hide on the first X-ray and lose its blood supply if missed.
1. Distal radius fracture

• What it is: a very common break of the end of the radius, usually from a FOOSH
    • upper-year notes: a Colles fracture (a complete break in the last 2 cm of the radius) is the most common forearm fracture
    • often comes with a torn ligament or a scaphoid fracture · if the anatomy is not restored, the wrist works poorly

rows: Ulnar variance on the front-to-back (PA) view: the ends of the radius and ulna compared
Neutral: both joint surfaces level (sources differ: upper-year notes say the radius is normally slightly longer - check the slides)
The radius collapses and shortens → positive ulnar variance · compare with the other wrist (some people have a short radius)
Ulna bumps into the carpal bones (ulnar impaction)
Volar tilt on the side (lateral) view
7-15° toward the palm, about 12° on average
Closer to 0°, or tilted toward the back
A step where the fracture enters the joint
A step over 1 mm leads to post-traumatic arthritis, pain and stiffness · correct it surgically

blocks.html:
• The medwiki note words positive variance as the ulna projecting further, then adds "radius longer than the ulna" in brackets, which contradicts itself (sources differ: the condition note and upper-year notes both tie positive variance to a shortened radius - check the slides)
  • Treatment depends on age
    • forgiving at the extremes: a young bone remodels itself straight · an older patient puts less load on the wrist and has laxer ligaments, so fewer symptoms
    • middle-aged or active patients need more intensive treatment
  • Closed reduction and casting
    • ① analgesia is essential: hematoma block (1% lidocaine into the fracture) · regional nerve block · conscious sedation
    • ② sustained pull along the bone (by hand or finger traps) relaxes the muscles
    • ③ manipulate: often make the deformity worse first to unlock the fragments, then correct it
    • ④ cast: cotton padding under plaster (cheap, mouldable, heavy) or fibreglass (can be waterproof, clearer on X-ray) · 3-point mould
    • ⑤ X-ray to confirm the alignment
  • Surgery if closed reduction fails: external fixation (pins through the skin held by rods, for a few weeks) · open reduction with plates and screws
  • Upper-year case: a displaced fracture plus tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers = acute carpal tunnel syndrome from the fragment pressing on the median nerve → open reduction, fixation and carpal tunnel release

blocks.html: 2. Scaphoid fracture

• What it is: the scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone · younger patients · FOOSH
    • many shrug it off as a sprain and it heals, but it is hard to diagnose, and a late diagnosis brings complications
  • Why it goes wrong: its blood enters at the far (distal) end and flows back toward the near end · a break through the middle cuts the proximal part off
  • Presents as: swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox · wrist pain · thumb pain, especially on the push-pull test of the thumb
  • Investigations
    • X-ray is usually enough, but can look normal
    • high suspicion with a normal X-ray: treat it as fractured, then repeat the X-ray in a couple of weeks (the fracture line shows as the bone heals) or go to CT, MRI or a bone scan
  • Treatment
    • cast: undisplaced fractures and distal-pole fractures · until healed, about 8 weeks (upper-year notes)
    • surgery (a screw): displaced fractures and proximal-pole fractures
  • Complications: non-union (does not heal) · osteonecrosis (bone death) · late arthritis, which may need a wrist fusion that costs flexion and extension
